title: Gestational Diabetes
bottomLine: GDM reflects pregnancy-related insulin resistance and increases fetal overgrowth, hypertensive, neonatal hypoglycemia and future type 2 diabetes risk. Monitor fasting/post-meal glucose, administer prescribed therapy safely, and make postpartum diabetes screening part of discharge planning.
recognize: Fetal overgrowth or maternal hypertensive risk
differentiate: GDM often resolves after delivery but future diabetes risk remains
One isolated glucose does not replace trend-based assessment
medicationSafety: Insulin needs can change rapidly during pregnancy and fall after delivery
Never change insulin solely because intake changed without following the diabetes plan
counselling: GDM is also a future diabetes risk marker
Keep postpartum testing even if glucose normalizes
followUp: Postpartum 75-g OGTT/diabetes follow-up per current Canadian plan
examTrap: Assuming GDM care ends when the placenta is delivered.
oneLinePearl: GDM ends as a pregnancy diagnosis, not as a lifetime diabetes risk.

title: Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes
bottomLine: PPROM is membrane rupture before labour and before 37 weeks. Major nursing threats are ascending infection, cord prolapse/compression, abruption and prematurity. Avoid unnecessary digital vaginal examination and escalate fever, uterine tenderness, fetal change, cord prolapse, bleeding or labour.
recognize: Gush or persistent leakage of fluid
Contractions may or may not be present
differentiate: Urinary leakage is not amniotic-fluid rupture
Term ROM has a different prematurity risk balance
management: Expectant management or delivery based on gestation and status
Immediate emergency delivery pathway for cord prolapse, infection or fetal compromise
medicationSafety: Do not delay emergency delivery just to finish a medication course
counselling: Report fever, foul fluid, bleeding, contractions or reduced movement
examTrap: Performing repeated routine digital exams after PPROM.
oneLinePearl: PPROM: protect from infection, watch the cord, respect prematurity.

title: Shoulder Dystocia
bottomLine: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed after the fetal head delivers and shoulders do not. Call for the team immediately, document head-delivery time and maneuvers, assist McRoberts/suprapubic pressure as directed, prepare neonatal resuscitation, and never apply fundal pressure.
recognize: Head delivers but shoulders fail with normal gentle traction
differentiate: It cannot be definitively diagnosed before the head delivers
Routine slow progress before head delivery is a different labour problem
workup: Clinical emergency—do not delay for imaging
management: Prepare neonatal resuscitation and postpartum hemorrhage response
medicationSafety: No medication relieves the mechanical impaction
counselling: Provide concise explanation during emergency and debrief afterward
followUp: Maternal trauma/bleeding and newborn neurologic assessment
oneLinePearl: Shoulder dystocia: call, clock, McRoberts, suprapubic—not fundal.

title: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
bottomLine: Screen at-risk newborns and check any symptomatic newborn immediately. CPS uses 2.6 mmol/L as a key intervention threshold for at-risk infants in the first 72 hours; symptomatic or persistent hypoglycemia needs prompt escalation beyond feeding alone.
differentiate: Normal newborn sleepiness should not explain poor feeding plus low glucose
Sepsis can mimic hypoglycemia and may coexist
assessment: Risk group: IDM, preterm, SGA/LGA, perinatal stress
management: 40% dextrose gel with feeding for selected asymptomatic cases
medicationSafety: Dextrose gel complements feeding rather than replacing it
Do not delay IV therapy in a symptomatic severe case
counselling: Explain feeding and repeat glucose plan
followUp: Ensure stable glucose and feeding before discharge
examTrap: Treating a lethargic newborn with feeding alone when urgent IV glucose is indicated.
oneLinePearl: Low glucose + symptoms = treat the baby, not just the number.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society neonatal hypoglycemia guidance updated 2025

title: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
bottomLine: Newborn bilirubin is interpreted by age in hours, gestational age and neurotoxicity risk—not one universal number. Jaundice in the first 24 hours or a sleepy poorly feeding jaundiced infant requires prompt assessment for pathologic hyperbilirubinemia.
differentiate: Physiologic jaundice occurs later and remains below treatment thresholds
Skin colour alone cannot quantify bilirubin
management: Escalate intensive therapy/exchange pathway when indicated
medicationSafety: Sunlight is not a substitute for prescribed phototherapy
Phototherapy requires thermoregulation and hydration monitoring
counselling: Explain bilirubin follow-up and feeding plan
Return urgently for neurologic or feeding deterioration
followUp: Repeat bilirubin based on discharge risk and treatment response
examTrap: Using one bilirubin cutoff for every newborn regardless of age and gestation.
oneLinePearl: Bilirubin only makes sense with the baby's age in hours and risk factors.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society hyperbilirubinemia guidance updated 2025
